sections.h2: Which office files a deed in Peoria County?
sections.html:
Land records sit with the County Clerk, in the courthouse at 324 Main Street, Room 101, Peoria, IL 61602. The Clerk's Land Records page gathers the deed index, transfer declarations and the current fee schedule in one place. Counter hours are half past eight to half past four, Monday through Friday, and the main line is (309) 672-6060.

The online index comes with a caution from the county itself: it works like a library card catalogue, pointing toward documents without standing in for them. Read the recorded deed, or have the title company order the chain of title, before trusting a name or a legal description that you saw only in the index.

sections.h2: Can a Peoria County deed be recorded electronically?
sections.html:
Yes. The county's e-Recording page names two approved submitters, Indecomm Global Services and Simplifile. Title companies, banks and law firms send documents through them, and the county reports that most come back recorded within 24 hours rather than the weeks or days a paper submission can take.

  • No postage, and no dash to the courthouse before the counter closes.
  • Fewer rejected documents, with corrections turned around sooner.

Anything that arrives outside one of those channels is handled on paper at the Clerk's office. Ask your closer early which path your sale will take.

sections.h2: Which forms travel with a deed recorded in Peoria County?
sections.html:
Form PTAX-203, the Illinois Real Estate Transfer Declaration, accompanies every deed. Peoria County joined the state's MyDec system, which lets the declaration be submitted online before recording. In the state's description, buyer and seller prepare the form together and file it with the county where the land lies.

Land inside the city of Peoria adds city paperwork, summarized here from the county and city pages.

Peoria deed paperwork, drawn from county Clerk and City of Peoria pages
DocumentWhen it appliesHow it is handled
PTAX-203 declarationDeeds anywhere in the countyOnline through MyDec, or at the Clerk
City transfer declarationParcels within Peoria city limitsTurned in alongside the deed
City exemption certificateWhen a city exemption is claimedSigned by the owner, agent or attorney
Zoning certificateCommercial or multi-family property where money is exchangedRequested from Community Development at City Hall

sections.h2: What transfer taxes apply when a Peoria County property sells?
sections.html:
Illinois imposes its own transfer tax, and the Department of Revenue points filers to its Tax Rate Database for the figure. Counties are allowed to levy a further 25 cents per $500 of value, and home rule cities may add theirs. The recorder collects by selling revenue stamps, which the county purchases from the state.

Peoria's city tax is $2.50 for each $1,000 of value, counting any fraction of $1,000, as stated on the declaration. An ordinance from 1989 created it, and the city's instruction sheet says it is paid at the county recording office. When a house keeps an existing mortgage, the state says the base counts only the owner's equity, provided the deed says so on its face. The stamp total moves with the stated value, so get the number from your closer before you sign.

sections.h2: Are Peoria County recording fees about to change?
sections.html:
They are. The county posted a notice that fees rise on January 1, 2027, and the Land Records page links both a fee schedule and predictable fees information. The Clerk can quote the exact charge for your document type and page count, which matters if a closing could straddle the new year.

Fees are assembled from several lines, so a closing statement may show more than one recording charge. Compare the Clerk's quote with your statement rather than assuming a single flat amount.

sections.h2: What else does the Clerk's land records office offer?
sections.html:
Three extras appear on the Land Records page. Fraud Guard is described as a simple way to avoid becoming a victim of property fraud. The Illinois Anti-Predatory Lending program is explained there too, and GIS maps of the county can be downloaded as PDFs. People who hold property they rarely visit, such as out-of-town landlords or heirs, will want to read the Fraud Guard description.

Taxes that went to sale are settled in this same office. Redemption defaults to two years after the sale, a buyer may extend to three, and a home of one to six units carries a minimum of two and a half years. Pay with cash, a cashier's check or a money order made out to the Peoria County Clerk. Personal, mortgage and title company checks are turned away. Ask the title company to fold the redemption amount into the payoff.

sections.h2: How does a recorded deed connect to the Peoria County tax bill?
sections.html:
Each parcel gets its own annual bill. For 2025 taxes the county scheduled mailing by May 1, 2026, with halves due June 9 and September 9. Not getting a bill does not excuse payment, so owners with nothing in hand by May 15 are told to phone the Treasurer.

The Clerk also computes each district's rate and posts levy, valuation and rate data by May 15 every year. A tax district search on the county site returns the districts for any address, and propertytax.peoriacounty.gov shows parcel details and bill history. Either office can say whether a prior year was sold before closing day.

sections.h2: What are the recent census numbers for Peoria County?
sections.html:
The Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate is 178,553 residents, down 1.9% from the 2020 base, across 84,884 housing units. Owners hold 67.0% of homes, with a 2020-2024 median value of $158,500. Median gross rent is $993 and median household income is $65,108.

  • The county has 618.73 square miles of land, or 293.9 residents per square mile.
  • About 34.9% of adults 25 and older have a bachelor's degree or more.
  • Workers average 19.2 minutes of travel to their jobs.
  • There were 4,168 employer establishments in 2023.

Inside the city of Peoria the owner share drops to 57.5%, so a deed there is more likely to involve a tenant in place at closing.

faqs.q: What is the address for recording a deed in Peoria County?
faqs.a: The County Clerk, 324 Main Street, Room 101, Peoria, IL 61602. Hours run from half past eight to half past four on weekdays, and the phone number is (309) 672-6060. Title companies and law firms can submit through Simplifile or Indecomm Global Services.

faqs.q: Is a transfer declaration required with a Peoria County deed?
faqs.a: Yes. Form PTAX-203 goes with the deed, and Peoria County accepts it through the state's MyDec system. Parcels in the city of Peoria also need the city's own declaration, plus an exemption certificate when a city exemption is claimed.

faqs.q: How is the City of Peoria transfer tax set?
faqs.a: The city's instruction sheet prints $2.50 for each $1,000 of value or fraction of $1,000 stated on the declaration. Payment is made at the county recording office. Commercial or multi-family transfers need a zoning certificate from City Hall as well.

faqs.q: Will Peoria County raise recording fees?
faqs.a: The county posted a notice of a fee increase on January 1, 2027. The Clerk's Land Records page carries the current schedule, and the Clerk can quote a price for your document before you submit it.

faqs.q: Who accepts payment to redeem sold taxes in Peoria County?
faqs.a: The County Clerk. Pay once, in full, with cash, a cashier's check or a money order made out to the Peoria County Clerk. Payment plans and partial payments are not allowed, and an online estimate shows the next penalty date.
